title: Sharpen a kitchen knife on a whetstone at 15 to 20 degrees, both sides, then lay it down edge away
instruction: Sharpen the knife on the whetstone, then put it back on the chopping block.
context: Sharpening a kitchen knife is a familiar household chore: a dull knife slips and needs more force, and many home cooks keep a whetstone for it, as do cooks and butchers who look after their own knives. The trained skill is the angle: the blade is held 15 to 20 degrees off the stone and drawn across it edge first, a few strokes on each face, then the knife is laid down flat with its edge away from the body. Held too flat, the stone grinds the face behind the bevel and never reaches the edge; held too steep, it grinds a more obtuse edge that cuts less keenly; sharpening one face only pushes the edge over into a wire instead of making it sharp. Sharpness is measured, not judged by eye: an edge tester reads the grams of force the edge needs to cut a standard test filament.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0; headings are measured from +x toward +y. Chopping block: an end-grain maple butcher block, 12 x 22 x 8 cm, fixed, its center at (16.4, 8.5), its long side at heading 105 degrees (turned 15 degrees from the y axis), its top at z 8. Knife: a 165 mm santoku (Japanese kitchen knife), 100 g, steel blade 16.5 cm long, 4.5 cm tall at the heel and 2 mm thick, its spine running straight for 7 cm and then curving down to the tip, its edge straight with a 6 mm rise over the last 3 cm to the tip, and a bright 6 mm ground bevel along the edge, an octagonal magnolia handle 9.5 cm long and 1.8 to 2.0 cm across with a dark horn ferrule; its balance point 2 cm in front of the bolster. It lies flat on the block, face A down, edge facing away from the robot (heading 15 degrees), the tip pointing left along the block, the bolster at (18.4, 0.8) and the front 3 cm of the handle on the block, the rest of the handle reaching past the block's right-hand edge toward (20.9, -8.4) so a hand can close round it. Whetstone: an orange 1000-grit combination stone, 18 x 6 x 2.5 cm, in a black rubber non-slip holder (21 x 8 x 1.5 cm with end clamps 3 cm tall) on a 6 cm wooden sharpening stand, all fixed, centered at (39.4, -5.5), its long side at heading -15 degrees (pointing away from the robot and slightly right), the stone's top at z 10. The left arm is not needed; both arms start at their home pose. For a real trial the edge starts dull in the same way every time: with the stone soaked, hold the knife upright, edge straight down on the stone, and draw the whole edge once along the stone's length, heel to tip, pressing about 5 N (500 g on a kitchen scale under the stone). This jointing pass grinds a flat of even width along the edge, seen under a lamp as a thin unbroken line of reflected light. Four points are marked with a dot on face B, just above the bevel, 2, 6, 10 and 14 cm from the heel. A BESS edge tester (for example an Edge-On-Up PT50B) then reads each point; every point must read 500 g or more (a dull kitchen knife), or the pass is repeated. The four readings are written down as the start.
scoring: The same ladder scores sim and real trials. A real trial measures the edge; the sim, which grinds no steel, counts sharpening strokes on the stone as its stand-in. Sharp, in a real trial: after the trial, with no stropping or deburring, the BESS edge tester reads each of the four marked points (2, 6, 10 and 14 cm from the heel); a point is sharp at 300 g or less, about a new kitchen knife's edge and what a 1000-grit stone gives. The knife starts at 500 g or more at every point. Put down safely: let go (no part of either gripper touching the knife; a gap of 2 mm or less between the knife and the gripper's own shape counts as touching), the knife lying flat on the block (faces within 20 degrees of level, edge within 1 cm of the block's top) with its edge within 60 degrees of facing away from the robot, so the next hand that reaches for the handle does not meet the edge. A real trial checks it on the top photo with a protractor. The trial scores 1.0 when the edge is sharpened along most of its length and the knife is put down safely and still for 1 s. In a real trial that means at least 3 of the 4 marked points read 300 g or less; in the sim, 3 or more strokes on each face and at least 12 of the scorer's 16 edge points (three quarters of the edge) worked on each face. It scores 0.75 when the edge is sharpened as for 1.0 but the knife is not put down safely (still held, left on the stone, or edge toward the robot). It scores 0.5 when only part of the edge is sharpened: in a real trial 1 or 2 marked points read 300 g or less; in the sim 3 or more strokes on each face but fewer than 12 points worked on a face. It scores 0.25 when the edge is sharper but not sharp: in a real trial no point reads 300 g or less but at least 3 read 100 g or more below their own start; in the sim 3 or more strokes on one face only, which pushes the edge over into a wire. Otherwise it scores 0, including when the robot does nothing (the knife stays dull). Where the arms end is not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. The sim's stroke: the knife held (both fingers of a gripper touching the handle, their opening stopped by its 1.8 to 2.0 cm girth), its edge lower than its spine and touching the stone (its lowest point within 0.5 mm of the stone's top), and moved 5 cm edge first in one touch while the sharpening angle (how far the blade's width tilts below the stone's top) is 13 to 22 degrees (15 to 20 degrees, plus 2 degrees each way for a hand), the blade's length is within 5 degrees of level, and at least 3 edge points (about 3 cm, half the stone's 6 cm width) are within 1 mm of the stone. Strokes count on the face that is down. The scorer checks 16 points about 1 cm apart, from 0.5 to 16.2 cm along the 16.5 cm edge; a point is worked on a face once it has been on the stone for 5 cm of such travel. Edge-trailing travel and travel flatter than 13 degrees do not count. A touch with 2 cm of travel steeper than 22 degrees (it grinds a more obtuse edge), or one that rolls off an end of the stone (the edge 3 mm below its top just past an end within 0.5 s of leaving it), counts toward nothing but does not zero the trial. These sim thresholds are a lower bound on the work, not a measured match to the tester: in a real trial the readings decide. The side video is filmed against 15, 20 and 22 degree cards to report the angle; the angle is not scored in a real trial.
reset_notes: Put the knife back flat on the block, face A down, edge away, bolster at (18.4, 0.8); the stone, holder, stand and block are fixed. For a real trial, soak the stone 10 minutes, dull the edge again with the jointing pass in the setup, and check that all four marked points read 500 g or more on the edge tester before starting.
fidelity: Nothing is ground: the sim scores strokes from the knife's pose on the stone (angle, contact, travel per edge point) as a stand-in for steel removed, and a real trial measures the edge with a BESS edge tester instead. The stone is dry and rigid. The knife is 100 g (a real one is about 140 g); box colliders follow the blade's outline. The stand is 6 cm tall so the wrist clears the bench.
